conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be your doctor during your stay. You're here to start hemodialysis, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been feeling more tired and short of breath lately, especially when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned swelling in your legs and itching too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my legs are swollen up to my knees, and the itching is all over. It’s been bothering me at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. With your kidney function being very low, fluid and waste build up, which can cause those symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been gaining weight, though I’m not sure how much. And I can’t lie flat because of my belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your polycystic kidneys are quite large, about the size of watermelons, which explains the abdominal pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard to find clothes that fit. But I’m glad we’re starting dialysis now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start your first session today. You have a fistula in your right arm, which is good—it means we can use it for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was placed a few months ago. Is it ready to use?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s mature and functioning well. We’ll begin hemodialysis shortly. You should feel better after a few sessions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after your first dialysis session?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit tired, but my breathing seems a little easier already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We removed about two liters of fluid today, which should help with your swelling and breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a lot! No wonder I feel lighter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll do two more sessions before you go home. Your blood pressure is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on a lot of medications. Will those change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your kidneys aren’t filtering drugs like before, some meds need to be stopped or adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Which ones are we stopping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping atenolol, valsartan, furosemide, iron, darbepoetin, and hectorol. Your dialysis center will manage anemia and bone health now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what about my blood pressure? I’m still on amlodipine and lisinopril?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are safer to continue. We stopped atenolol because your heart rate was low—likely from the drug building up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on atenolol for my atrial fibrillation. Is that still under control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG showed sinus bradycardia, not afib. We’ll keep amiodarone and coumadin. Your INR is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And coumadin—I need to keep that monitored, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your dialysis center will manage your coumadin now. If not, contact your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a chest X-ray yesterday to make sure your heart and lungs are ready for dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And? Is everything okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your heart is at the upper limit of normal size, but no fluid in the lungs. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. How’s my second dialysis session going to be different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Similar to the first. We’ll remove more fluid and clean your blood. You’re tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve now had two sessions. How are you feeling overall?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My legs are less swollen, and I’m sleeping better. The itching is still there, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The itching may take a few more sessions to improve. We’ve started nephrocaps for your vitamins.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PPD test you placed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a TB screening. You’ll need to have it read at your primary doctor’s office in a couple days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed three dialysis sessions and are doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your new medications as listed. Most are now at bedtime. Your next dialysis is scheduled for Monday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel confused or nauseated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor right away. Those could be signs your levels are off. Otherwise, keep your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You did well. We’ll see you at your next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel stable. A bit weak, but better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body is adjusting. Keep up with your diet and fluid limits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that. And I’ll get the PPD test read.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re cleared to go home. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll be in touch with your dialysis team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we discussed DNR/DNI. You’re comfortable with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I don’t want aggressive resuscitation. I want comfort care if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s documented in your chart. Thank you for discussing that with us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate your respect for my wishes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s part of good care. Let’s get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse go over your meds and instructions one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to make sure I get it right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re here to support you every step of the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much more confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You're here today for your scheduled bilateral nephrectomy due to your polycystic kidney disease. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit nervous, but I’ve been in pain for months. I can’t bend or move well. I just want relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The surgery should help with the pain and mobility. We’ll remove both kidneys and repair the hernias we know about. The procedure is complex due to adhesions, but Dr. ___ will be doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on dialysis right after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start hemodialysis as scheduled. Your access is ready. We’ll monitor you closely, especially for blood pressure changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re back from surgery. The bilateral nephrectomy and hernia repair went well. The kidneys were very large—about 8 kg total. We spared your adrenal glands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I feel groggy, but no pain yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing okay overall, but we noticed you were more lethargic this morning and your temperature is up to 101.6. We’re concerned and ordering a brain MRI to rule out stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stroke? But I didn’t have weakness or slurred speech.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s reassuring. But confusion after surgery can be a sign, so we’re being cautious. We also drew blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the MRI and MRA of your head showed no stroke, bleeding, or blockage. Your mental status change isn’t from a brain issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s causing the confusion then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. It could be from infection, medications, or your body adjusting after surgery. Blood cultures are still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back negative. No infection in the blood. But we’re starting your first hemodialysis session today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous. I felt dizzy during dialysis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow. You did get a bit hypotensive, so we gave a fluid bolus. We’re adjusting the plan with cardiology to manage your atrial fibrillation and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve developed diarrhea. We sent a stool test for C. difficile, given your recent antibiotics and hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been watery and frequent. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your condition. We’re starting Flagyl while we wait for results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The test came back positive for C. diff. We’re upgrading to dual therapy—IV Flagyl and oral vancomycin—for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need this at home too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Infectious disease recommends continuing oral vancomycin after discharge to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis was tough again—you dropped pressure and needed fluids. This is partly due to the diarrhea causing fluid loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there anything we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology suggests holding your atenolol on dialysis mornings to avoid low BP. We’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still having ascites—fluid in your belly. Hepatology thinks it’s from low blood pressure and possible liver cyst compression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be making me feel bloated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. A liver ultrasound showed normal blood flow but many cysts and a lot of fluid. We may need to drain some.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your C. diff diarrhea is still severe. We’re continuing the dual antibiotics. The vancomycin is helping, but slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so tired from going to the bathroom all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’re supporting you with fluids and monitoring electrolytes. It should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A repeat abdominal X-ray shows no bowel obstruction. Your liver cyst is still there, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your stool tests today show improvement. No more C. diff toxin. But we’re keeping you on vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the infection is responding. But the diarrhea hasn’t fully stopped yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still having ascites. We’re starting midodrine to help with blood pressure and dialysis tolerance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me keep fluid off during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. It helps your blood vessels stay constricted, so you’re less likely to drop pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a paracentesis today—drained 3 liters of fluid from your abdomen. You should feel less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel better. My breathing is easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The fluid wasn’t infected—WBC was low. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has finally improved. Stools are less frequent and more formed. That’s a big milestone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it’s been over two weeks. I’m so glad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. You’ll continue oral vancomycin at home for two more weeks to prevent relapse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture showed some yeast, but it’s likely just from your mouth. No treatment needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had mouth sores. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll keep an eye on it. Good oral hygiene is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your incision looks great—no redness or drainage. We removed the clips and put on steri-strips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels better. No pain with movement now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’ve come a long way—surgery, infection, dialysis challenges, and ascites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re ready for discharge. We’re sending you home with services. You’ll continue dialysis as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take amiodarone, warfarin, levothyroxine, sevelamer, simvastatin, Prilosec, aspirin, and midodrine as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And continue the oral vancomycin for two more weeks. Take atenolol later in the day, not on dialysis mornings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever, chills, worsening diarrhea, belly pain, or swelling. Also if you can’t keep food or meds down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Cardiology wants a surface echo to check your heart function and help explain the low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis team will draw labs weekly until stable. They’ll adjust your meds based on results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve worked hard. We’re proud of your progress. Take care, and call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of worsening shortness of breath. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been getting worse since my last surgery. Last night, I could barely breathe while sitting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned chest pressure with it, but no pain or sweating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. It feels tight when I can’t catch my breath, but no sharp pain or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG shows you’re in atrial flutter, a fast heart rhythm. That could be making your heart work harder and causing fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had atrial fibrillation before. Is this the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s similar—both are irregular rhythms. This one is more organized but still too fast. We gave you some medication to slow it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the breathing trouble—could that be from my lungs or heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows small fluid collections around the lungs and possibly around the heart. But no pneumonia. This fluid is likely from heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s my heart not pumping well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re concerned your heart function has worsened, possibly due to the fast rhythm over time. We’ll check with an echocardiogram.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The echo is back. Your heart’s pumping ability has declined—ejection fraction is now about 29%, down from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s not good, is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, yes. But the good news is this may be partly due to the fast heart rate. If we control the rhythm, your heart might recover.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What can we do about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging for a procedure called cardioversion—a controlled shock to reset your heart rhythm. But first, we need a transesophageal echo to check for clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s routine. You’ll be sedated. We do it to make sure it’s safe to do the cardioversion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was low when you came in—1.8—so we increased your warfarin dose to 4 mg daily to reduce clot risk before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 2 mg. Is 4 mg safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially since your last INR was therapeutic. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re scheduled for dialysis today. We’ll remove extra fluid, which should help your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually feel better after dialysis. How much fluid will they take off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They plan to remove about 3.5 liters. That should relieve the pressure on your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling after dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can breathe easier already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The fluid was definitely contributing. We’ll do another session later this week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have another dialysis session today with ultrafiltration to remove more fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely. You’re on midodrine, which helps with low BP during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. The EP team is ready to proceed with the TEE and cardioversion tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little nervous about the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. You’ll be asleep the whole time. The team will check for clots first, then do the cardioversion if it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did great yesterday. The TEE showed no clots, and the cardioversion was successful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m in normal rhythm now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re in sinus rhythm. Your heart rate is around 80—much better than the 110-120 you were having.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Will it stay this way?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on amiodarone and metoprolol to help maintain it. You’ll need close follow-up with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re breathing well and your heart rhythm is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you from atenolol to metoprolol twice daily. It’s better for rate control in your case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the amlodipine I take on non-dialysis days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping that. Your blood pressure is well-controlled, and it’s not needed anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 3 mg daily now—down from 4 mg—until your INR is checked next week. Then we’ll adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue taking it as prescribed until you see your infectious disease doctor. No diarrhea so far, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep my dialysis appointments on Monday, Wednesday, Friday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, resume your regular schedule tomorrow. Call if you have any breathing issues or chest discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up with cardiology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have an appointment to reassess your heart function in two weeks. They’ll check if your ejection fraction has improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be home within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check—any chest pressure or shortness of breath since the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. I feel like I can take a full breath for the first time in weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Your heart and lungs are responding well to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge summary is ready. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take my meds and keep my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call us if anything changes. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in with shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started two days ago. I couldn’t lie flat and felt like I had to burp, but it was more in my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds uncomfortable. Was it similar to past episodes when your heart rhythm was off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly like that. But this time it lasted longer, so I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. I see you missed your dialysis yesterday because of the holiday?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I knew I’d feel a bit puffy, but I didn’t expect this much trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That likely contributed. Fluid builds up when you miss dialysis, and with your heart condition, it can cause shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on amiodarone and metoprolol since my last episode. Is my heart rhythm okay now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your EKG shows you’re in normal sinus rhythm. No atrial fibrillation right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why the chest pressure then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s due to heart failure worsening from fluid overload and your mitral valve leak. Your ejection fraction is around 40-45%, which is reduced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. Your troponin is normal, and the EKG doesn’t show ischemia. It’s more likely decompensated heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my potassium? I remember it was high in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was 6.9 on admission — quite high. But you didn’t have EKG changes, so we gave calcium, insulin, and sugar to shift it into cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll recheck after dialysis. It should come down once we remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows small pleural effusions and some atelectasis at the bases — consistent with fluid overload, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that clear up with dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as we remove fluid, your lungs should improve. You’ll have dialysis today around noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I also felt lightheaded earlier. Is that from my heart rate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate was 52, and you mentioned dizziness. We’re lowering your metoprolol from 50mg twice daily to 37.5mg to see if that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been trying to cut back with my cardiologist anyway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also held your warfarin. Your INR was 4.6 — too high, increases bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on 3mg, but they changed it to 2mg in the ER. Should I stay on that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it held today. Before discharge, we’ll check your INR again and restart at a safe dose, likely 2mg daily if it’s below 3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can breathe easier already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We removed about 3 liters — that should help your heart work better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show potassium is now 4.6 — perfect. Creatinine and urea are also down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the dialysis really helped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it corrected the potassium and reduced fluid. Your breathing and chest pressure should keep improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I be worried about my mitral valve? It’s been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s moderate to severe, and we discussed it with your cardiologist. For now, we’ll manage it medically. Surgery isn’t urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart failure — anything new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend starting an ACE inhibitor after discharge to help your heart function long-term. Discuss it with your cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8 — safe to restart warfarin at 2mg daily. We’ll send you home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What about my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue amiodarone, levothyroxine, sevelamer, and aspirin. We’re cutting omeprazole in half and reducing midodrine to 10mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And metoprolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 37.5mg twice daily — that’s one and a half of the 25mg tablets.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting. Keep monitoring your weight and symptoms. Call if you have chest pain, trouble breathing, or dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your cardiologist in a week. They may want a heart monitor to check for silent arrhythmias.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. We’re discharging you home in stable condition. Keep up with dialysis and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check — you’re still feeling well, no chest pain or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m good. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — should I watch for bleeding with the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially in the first few days. Report any unusual bruising, nosebleeds, or dark stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll check my INR as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge orders are signed. A nurse will go over instructions and medications one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care and stay on schedule with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hopefully not! Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your transplant team doctors. You’re here for your kidney transplant, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been waiting for this for a long time. I’m a little nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. You’re in good hands. We’ll do some final blood work tonight and plan to take you to surgery tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. Will I be okay during the surgery? I have atrial fibrillation and I’m on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history. Your Coumadin was stopped as planned before surgery. We’ll monitor your heart closely. You’ve had episodes of fast heart rate before, so we’re prepared for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my thyroid? I take levothyroxine every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep you on your usual dose. We’ll check your thyroid levels during your stay just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. Everything went smoothly. You had the kidney transplant and the hernia repair with mesh.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. Did the kidney start working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It had good color and blood flow, but it didn’t make urine right away. That can happen. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt my heart racing earlier. Is that why I’m in the ICU?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were in atrial fibrillation with a fast heart rate. We gave you medication through your IV to help control it. You’re on amiodarone and metoprolol now, just like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m feeling a little better now. What about my potassium? It’s always high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was high—6.7—so we did an emergency dialysis session last night. You’ll have another one today to keep it under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Will I keep needing dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, yes. We’re hoping the new kidney starts working soon. If it does, we’ll stop dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your heart rate is more stable today. We’re switching you from the IV amiodarone to your regular pill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How’s the kidney doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still not making much urine—less than 50 cc in 24 hours. But the ultrasound showed good blood flow, no blockages. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it might just be slow to start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We call that delayed graft function. It happens sometimes, especially with ECD kidneys. We’ll keep supporting you with dialysis for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re being moved to the regular floor today. Your heart rate stayed stable overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I feel stronger. But I had some jaw pain and my arm felt heavy earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and enzymes. No sign of a heart attack. You were in atrial fibrillation again, but your rate is controlled. Cardiology recommends adding IV metoprolol when needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it wasn’t my heart. But I’m tired of being in AFib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. But as long as your rate is controlled and you’re not having chest pain, we’ll manage it with meds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs look stable. Potassium is 5.2. You’re still not making much urine, but your weight is up, so we’re watching your fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad—weight going up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Since the kidney isn’t filtering yet, fluid builds up. But your breathing is fine, so we’re okay for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big news—your urine output increased today! You made about 300 cc in 24 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Really? That’s a good sign, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes! It means the kidney is starting to wake up. We’ll keep an eye on your creatinine and see if it starts to drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made 500 cc of urine yesterday! Creatinine is still high, but stable. We’re not planning more dialysis unless needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s amazing. When will I know if the kidney is really working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll know more in the next few days. If output keeps rising and creatinine drops, we’ll be confident it’s functioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You made 750 cc of urine yesterday! Creatinine is 6.5—still high, but not rising. This is a great step forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t believe it. I’m so relieved. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tacrolimus level was 11.6, which is a bit high, so we lowered the dose to 5 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Cellcept? It’s been giving me heartburn.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched you to Myfortic. It’s similar but easier on the stomach. You’ve been tolerating it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Can I restart my Coumadin? I’m worried about clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re restarting warfarin tonight. Since the kidney is making urine, we don’t need to worry about a biopsy, so it’s safe to restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my thyroid? You said you checked it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your TSH is low—0.2—but your free T4 is normal. It might be from the amiodarone. Keep taking your levothyroxine and follow up with your PCP after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve had bowel movements, you’re eating regular food—just low potassium for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bananas or potatoes, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Avoid tomatoes, oranges, and dark greens too. Drink plenty of fluids so your urine stays light yellow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If all goes well, tomorrow. We’ll make sure your pain is controlled and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful! What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your meds as prescribed. You’ll get Myfortic, tacrolimus, warfarin, and others. Check your urine output daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Only as needed. Don’t drive while taking it. And no lifting more than 5 pounds for several weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my incision?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can shower—just pat it dry. No lotions. Watch for redness, drainage, or fever. Call the clinic if any of that happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Blood work every Monday and Thursday—CBC, chem panel, tacrolimus level. Send results to the transplant clinic. INR goes to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. The kidney is starting to work, and you’re on the right track. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just so grateful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad to see you doing well. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your nystatin is for a possible mouth infection. Use it four times a day as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll start that today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And the docusate—just to help with constipation from the pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take it twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over your discharge papers and get you on your way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep following up, and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m so thankful for the new kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hopeful it will keep improving. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call if I have any problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please do. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it one day at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be helping take care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling really off. I had diarrhea for a few days, but that stopped last night. Now I have a headache, dizziness, and pain in my left lower belly. Also, my feet hurt—like a burning and itching feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And I understand you’ve been having some other symptoms—your daughter mentioned hallucinations?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, just a little—like shadows moving. I was worried. And I’ve been tired, with no appetite, just feel full all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. You’ve had a kidney transplant recently, and you’re on several medications, including Prograf. Your level came back very high—23—so you were told to hold a dose. That might be contributing to how you’re feeling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that could be why I’m dizzy and seeing things? I was scared it was something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. High Prograf levels can affect the brain. We’ve lowered your dose to 3mg twice a day for now, and we’ll check it again tomorrow. That should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. But what about the belly pain? It’s near my JP drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We examined you—the area is red and warm, tracking from the drain site. That suggests cellulitis, a skin infection. We’ll start antibiotics for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before, after my hernia surgery. Is it MRSA again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think so this time. We’re starting doxycycline, which covers common skin bacteria. We’ll monitor how it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my urine test showed an infection too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have a UTI caused by E. coli. It’s resistant to some antibiotics, so we started IV ceftriaxone. Once we know the best oral option, we’ll switch you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad we caught it. I didn’t even have burning or urgency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with transplant patients—your symptoms can be subtle. We’re also watching your kidney function. Your creatinine is up a bit, but we think it’s due to the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my feet? The redness and pain—is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed the redness on the soles. It could be related to circulation or a side effect of medications. We’ll keep an eye on it. For now, we don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my JP drain—output is down to 20ml a day. Should we remove it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign—low output means it’s ready to come out. The urology team will remove your ureteral stent tomorrow, and we’ll assess the drain then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I just want to feel like myself again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back clean—no bacteria in the blood. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. How’s the UTI looking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sensitivity testing showed the E. coli is sensitive to cefpodoxime. We’ll switch you to that oral antibiotic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stent removal—is that today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, later this morning. It’s a quick procedure at the bedside. It might help with your flank and belly discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope so. The pain’s been nagging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stent is out. You did great. Any pain now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just a little sore, but much better than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep you on doxycycline for the cellulitis and switch to cefpodoxime for the UTI. Your Prograf level this morning was 11.1—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go back to my regular dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll keep it at 3mg twice a day for now. The transplant team will call you tonight with long-term adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my INR? I’m on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable. You’ll take 1mg tonight, and they’ll check it again tomorrow to guide your next dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking better. The redness around your abdomen is improving, and you’re afebrile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Headache’s gone, and I’m eating a little more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your labs show improvement—creatinine is down to 3.1, and white count is normalizing. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue mycophenolate, valganciclovir, levothyroxine, and metoprolol. Omeprazole is now 20mg twice a day. And you’ll take doxycycline for 7 days and cefpodoxime for 12.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Prograf?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue 3mg twice a day until the transplant team calls with further instructions. They’ll call you tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Output is low—20ml/day—so we’ll remove it before you go home. We’ll give you instructions on how to care for the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my feet? Still a little red.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s related to circulation or medication. It’s not spreading, so we’ll monitor it as an outpatient. Wear comfortable shoes and report any worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home. The drain is out, and you’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the transplant clinic if you have fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Watch the incision for redness, drainage, or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get a full list. Take cefpodoxime daily for 12 days, doxycycline every 12 hours for 7. The transplant team will call tonight about your Prograf. Take only 1mg of Coumadin tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll wait for their call. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. You’ve made great progress. Rest, follow up, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember, home health will draw your Prograf level and INR tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I have it scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep taking your meds as directed and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge paperwork is ready. You’re cleared to leave whenever you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you so much. I feel much safer going home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re all set to go? Transportation is here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my daughter’s outside. Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in today because of some weight gain and lab changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve gained about 5 pounds in the last couple of days. I didn’t change my diet or anything. My regular labs showed my creatinine was up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We just got your ultrasound results. There’s swelling in the kidney from your transplant — it’s called hydronephrosis. That’s likely why your creatinine is rising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious? The kidney’s not draining?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The ureter — the tube from the kidney to the bladder — seems blocked, probably from inflammation or swelling. We’ll need to place a temporary tube to drain the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A tube? Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s called a percutaneous nephrostomy. You’ll get light sedation, and it’s done with ultrasound guidance. It’s very safe and will help protect your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today. The interventional radiology team is ready. After that, we’ll monitor your labs and see how the kidney responds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. The procedure went smoothly. The nephrostomy tube is in place and draining urine well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean the blockage is fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not completely. They tried to thread the tube all the way into the bladder, but there was too much swelling. So for now, it’s draining externally into a bag.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so I’ll have this bag for a while?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just temporarily. In a few days, they’ll try again to advance it into the bladder. For now, the important thing is that your kidney is draining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the infection I was on antibiotics for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were on cefpodoxime for a suspected UTI. We sent a urine sample from the nephrostomy tube to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It grew VRE — that’s a type of resistant enterococcus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: VRE? I’ve heard that’s tough to treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, but we have an effective antibiotic — linezolid. It works well against VRE and can be taken by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I stop the cefpodoxime?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re stopping it. It won’t work against VRE. You’ll start linezolid twice a day for 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine was 2.7 when you came in. This morning it’s 2.4 — that’s a good sign the drainage is helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Does that mean the kidney is recovering?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a positive trend. We’ll keep monitoring it. You’re also passing small amounts of urine on your own, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, your labs are stable today. Creatinine is still 2.4. The nephrostomy tube is draining well, and you’re feeling okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no pain, I’m eating and walking. But I’m worried about being on Coumadin. Is it safe with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good question. We’re holding your Coumadin for now. The tube site could bleed, so we’ll restart it only after the next procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. When will they try to move the tube into the bladder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be scheduled for a nephrogram in the next few days — they’ll inject contrast to see the ureter and try to advance the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat urine culture today showed no growth. That means the linezolid is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful news. So the infection is clearing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and you’ll finish the full 10-day course at home to make sure it stays gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well — stable labs, eating, moving around. We’d like to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the linezolid twice daily for 10 days. Keep the nephrostomy bag empty and watch for fever, pain, or decreased output.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are the same. We’re adding furosemide to help with fluid balance and adjusting your metoprolol and levothyroxine doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still hold it. The transplant team will tell you when to restart after the next procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with them. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have fevers, chills, chest pain, or any drop in urine output — from either the tube or your own voiding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad we caught this early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. The tube helped prevent further kidney damage. You’re going home in good shape.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check — you’re alert, no pain, vitals stable. We’ll get your discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — should I watch for any side effects from linezolid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. It can cause nausea or headache. Rarely, it affects blood counts or nerves with long use. But 10 days is safe for most people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll watch for that and call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re very attentive — that helps a lot with recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I shower with the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but keep the site dry. Use a waterproof cover or plastic wrap. Don’t submerge it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And how often should I empty the bag?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Every 4 to 6 hours, or when it’s half full. Make sure it’s below your kidney level when you’re sitting or lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You handled this really well. Take care at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — I’ll get a call about the nephrogram appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, interventional radiology will contact you within the next few days to schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you had sudden pain in your transplanted kidney earlier today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started in my lower right side and spread across my belly and up into my chest. I was sweating and it didn’t go away for almost an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds very uncomfortable. The good news is the pain went away before you got here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it suddenly stopped on the way in the ambulance. I feel okay now, just worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. We’re going to run some tests, including an ultrasound of your transplanted kidney, to see if there’s any blockage or other issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been tracking my urine output. It’s less than before, but total is around 1100 mL a day between the tube and voiding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ll monitor that closely. Any fever, nausea, or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. But I’ve had loose greenish stools since starting linezolid for the VRE infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a known side effect. We’ll keep an eye on it. Let’s get the ultrasound done and go from there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. There’s still hydronephrosis in the transplanted kidney. The nephrostomy tube is in a calyx but not clearly in the renal pelvis, so it might not be draining well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the tube isn’t working right? Could that be why I had pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The blockage may have caused pressure to build up. We’re scheduling a nephrostogram tomorrow to check the tube and possibly place a stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A stent? What does that do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small tube that goes from the kidney to the bladder, bypassing the blockage. It should help drain urine properly and prevent future pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Will I be awake for it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get light sedation, so you’ll be relaxed but not fully asleep. The radiologist will guide everything with imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re about to start the nephrostogram. The team will check the current tube and place a stent if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready. Just let me know what’s happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — the procedure went well. We confirmed the nephrostomy tube had pulled back, and there was a blockage in the upper ureter. We placed an 8 Fr x 10 cm stent across it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the blockage is fixed? Does that mean I’m better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stent should relieve the obstruction. Your creatinine was 2.9 on admission — we’ll watch it closely to see if it improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 2.6 today — that’s a good sign the kidney is draining better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. But I’ve been feeling some jaw and shoulder pain, and burning in my chest, especially when I lie down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your cardiac enzymes four times — all negative. EKG shows your usual atrial fibrillation, but no signs of heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The pain improving when you sit up suggests reflux. We’ve consulted GI. They recommend continuing omeprazole and nystatin for thrush.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on omeprazole before. Should I take more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing it to 40 mg twice daily. We may do an endoscopy later to check for esophagitis, but your symptoms are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is now 2.5. Still not where we want it, so we’re planning a kidney biopsy tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? Is something wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s to check if there’s rejection or other damage. Since your creatinine isn’t dropping fast, we want to be sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. Do I need to stop any meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re already off Coumadin, which helps. The biopsy is low risk, and we’ll do it with ultrasound guidance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy is done. No signs of rejection, which is excellent. But we did see donor disease, which means the kidney had some pre-existing changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not rejection, but the kidney wasn’t perfect to start with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That explains why recovery is slower. The stent should help, and we’ll keep supporting kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried capping your nephrostomy tube yesterday, but you had low urine output and a burning sensation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, only 50 cc when I tried to void. Then 120 cc came out when you uncapped the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you were dehydrated — you were NPO for the possible endoscopy. We gave fluids, and your output improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I need to stay hydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very important. We’ll keep the tube open for now and reassess as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my Coumadin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted it yesterday. Your INR will be checked soon, and your PCP will manage it going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 2.4 — best we’ve seen. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the nephrostomy tube open to gravity drainage and record output daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if something seems wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the transplant office if you have fever, chills, pain, redness, or decreased output. Also, keep taking linezolid for the full 10 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about the green stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Should improve after you finish the antibiotic. Stay hydrated and eat small, frequent meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heartburn?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue omeprazole twice daily and nystatin for thrush. Follow up with GI in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any other tests before I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked G6PD today because of your allergy to Bactrim. It’ll help us choose the right infection prevention med.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember — I had palpitations with pentamidine before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right, so we’re being careful. We’ll decide on dapsone or another option based on the result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge. Your condition is stable, and you’re feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — get your labs drawn as scheduled and follow up with your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad the pain’s gone and the kidney is working better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad too. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll see you then. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're doing great. Just keep up with the care plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve learned a lot this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best outcome — staying informed and healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re ready to send you off. Take it easy and call if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll be here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I feel safe knowing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re here for. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. No rushing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s the best medicine right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I agree. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the surgical team doctors. I understand you came in after having your nephrostomy tube replaced this morning and then developed some pain and chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. Right after I got home, I had this sharp pain in my lower belly that went to my right side. And I’ve been feeling feverish and nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned some burning when you urinate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since the tube was changed. It wasn’t like that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history with the transplanted kidney and the recent procedure, we’re concerned about a possible infection. We’ve started you on an antibiotic called linezolid just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the tube change? I was worried something went wrong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common after procedures like this. The manipulation can introduce bacteria. We’re being cautious because you’ve had infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. My daughter said I’ve seemed really down lately. I just feel so tired of being in and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We actually spoke with your daughter, and we’ve requested a psychiatry consult to help support you emotionally during this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’d really like to talk to someone. My grandson is in the NICU, and I feel like I’m not even helping my family right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a lot to carry. We’ll make sure you get the support you need. For now, let’s focus on getting the infection under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back — it shows E. coli, which is a common bacteria. The good news is it’s not resistant, so we can switch you to a different antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I’ve heard of E. coli from food poisoning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same bacteria, but here it’s causing a urinary tract infection. Since you have a stent and tube, it can travel up more easily. We’ll treat it with cefpodoxime, an oral antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay in the hospital for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you a bit longer to make sure the fever doesn’t come back and that you’re tolerating the medication. Your white blood cell count is normal, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The new antibiotic made me a little nauseous earlier. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, that might be from another medication — atovaquone. It’s for pneumonia prevention, but it can cause nausea. We’re switching you to dapsone instead, which should be easier on your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried I was reacting badly to everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. We’re adjusting based on how you respond. Your kidney function is stable — creatinine is 2.2, and today it’s down to 2.1. That’s a good trend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed some leakage around your nephrostomy tube again. That’s not ideal — it can increase infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
