conversation_lines.text: It’s been dripping more since yesterday. Is the tube loose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Imaging suggests the stent may have shifted. We recommend replacing the tube again to ensure proper drainage and stop the leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another procedure? Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a quick procedure under light sedation. You’ll be comfortable. We’ll use imaging to guide it and make sure the new tube is placed correctly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. I just want this to stop happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you did great this morning. The tube was replaced successfully. The old one had migrated — the pigtail wasn’t in the right place, which caused the leak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why it wasn’t working right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The new one is positioned well — contrast showed good flow into the bladder and no leakage. That should help prevent more infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve been so worried about getting sick again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. That’s why we’re being thorough. Your latest labs look good — creatinine is now 1.9, which is your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The psychiatrist came by earlier. It helped just to talk. They said I’m coping well, considering everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m really glad you spoke with them. Emotional health is part of your recovery. We’ll make sure you have follow-up support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re doing well. No fever, eating normally, and the tube isn’t leaking. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep the tube open to gravity drainage and record your output daily. Call the transplant office if you have fever, increased pain, redness, or less urine from the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue your usual doses — tacrolimus, mycophenolate, warfarin, and the others. Plus, the new antibiotic cefpodoxime for 10 days, and dapsone instead of atovaquone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them. Should I watch for any side effects?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With dapsone, watch for rash or shortness of breath — but it’s usually well-tolerated. The antibiotic might cause mild stomach upset. Take it with food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my weight — I’ve lost a few pounds. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve lost about 4 pounds since discharge, but your kidney function is stable. Keep monitoring it. If you keep losing weight or feel weaker, let us know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I just want to get back to feeling normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the right track. The transplant team will follow up with your tacrolimus levels. And keep in touch with your counselor — your mental health matters just as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate how you’ve explained everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here to support you. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another tube change soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. We’ll monitor you. The goal is to keep it stable. If there are no leaks or infections, you may go several weeks before the next one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds manageable. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have you out soon. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Rest well, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we aim for. Knowledge helps you take control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep recording my outputs and call if anything seems off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’re doing a great job managing your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for not rushing me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You deserve the time. We’re a team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like I can handle this now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Stay in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this hospital stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling awful—fever, shaking, and I passed out the other day. My urine turned red, and now it burns when I pee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you passed out—was that after you capped your nephrostomy tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. They told me to cap it, and then I started feeling dizzy and had to lie down. I came in when the fever hit 103.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. We’re concerned about a urinary tract infection, especially with your transplant history. We’ve uncapped your tube to help drainage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that. Is the infection in the kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your creatinine is elevated, which means your kidney isn’t filtering as well right now. We’re treating it as a transplant-related UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that get better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we expect it will. We’ve started IV antibiotics—linezolid and ceftriaxone—to cover the most likely bacteria, especially since you’ve had resistant infections before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember linezolid from last time. It made me tired. Is there another option?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using it temporarily. Once we know the exact bacteria, we can switch to something more targeted. We’ll monitor how you respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. My heart’s been racing too. Is that from the fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. You’re in atrial fibrillation, which we already manage with amiodarone and metoprolol. We’ll keep an eye on your rate. Your INR was high this morning, so we’ll adjust your warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High INR? I didn’t know that could happen so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Infections and changes in diet or meds can affect it. We’ll lower your dose to 2.5 mg daily and recheck in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my blood pressure? I know I’m on Lasix, but my legs were swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your Lasix because your kidney function was down. Now that we’re treating the infection, we’ll restart it at a lower dose once things stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just don’t want to get too swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your weight and symptoms closely. For now, focus on resting and letting the antibiotics work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your ultrasound came back—your transplanted kidney looks structurally normal, no abscess. But there’s variable blood flow in the upper pole, so we’ll need a follow-up scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No abscess? That’s a relief. But what does ‘variable flow’ mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means the blood isn’t flowing as smoothly in one area. It could be related to your stricture or scarring. We’ll watch it, but it’s not an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the infection? Any results yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—your urine culture grew Klebsiella, but it’s sensitive to many antibiotics. We’re switching from IV ceftriaxone to oral cefpodoxime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can take pills now? That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Eventually. We’ll finish a few more doses IV, then transition you fully. You’ll take cefpodoxime for 14 days after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And linezolid? Do I still need that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping it. Since Klebsiella is the only bug and it’s not resistant, we don’t need broad coverage anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I was worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable. We always aim to use the narrowest effective treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Fever’s gone, white count is still low but trending up. Creatinine dropped from 2.5 to 2.1.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? I feel less shaky today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Your body’s fighting the infection. We’re restarting Lasix at 40 mg once daily to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only once a day now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because your kidney function isn’t fully back. We don’t want to over-diurese you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. What about my Myfortic? I know it affects immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reduced it to 360 mg twice daily to lower infection risk while you’re recovering. Tacrolimus stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart murmur? You listened to my chest yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we heard a new diastolic component. Given your syncope, we did an echo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No valve infection or new structural issues. But your pulmonary hypertension has worsened slightly. It’s likely from chronic lung changes and heart strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something we monitor. It’s not acute, but we’ll follow up with cardiology to optimize your management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your infection is under control, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take cefpodoxime twice daily for 11 more days. Keep your nephrostomy tube uncapped. We’ll schedule a repeat urine culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Myfortic is now twice daily, metoprolol twice daily, warfarin at 2.5 mg—get your INR checked in a few days. Restart Lasix today at 40 mg once daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll write that down. Any activity limits?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can resume normal activities, but weigh yourself daily. Call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Transplant clinic in one week. Cardiology will reach out about the echo. And we’ve set you up for knee PT—you mentioned pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been bothering me. Thanks for getting that set up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’ve been through a lot—take it easy, follow the plan, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling dizzy and had very low blood pressure at home. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve been feeling off for about two weeks—like I had the flu, with body aches and no energy. A few days ago, I started getting lightheaded when I stood up. The day I came in, my blood pressure was 70 over something—I almost passed out in the shower.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned nausea and poor appetite, but no chest pain or headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. No chest pain. I’ve been forcing myself to eat. I did have some watery diarrhea today, but no belly pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We also know from your transplant team that you were recently found to have CMV in your blood. That’s a virus that can cause flu-like symptoms, especially in transplant patients. Your level was quite high—72,400 copies per mL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s why I’ve felt so sick? I was taken off valcyte because my white blood cells were low, but I didn’t realize it could come back like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s likely that stopping the antiviral allowed the CMV to reactivate. We’re starting you on IV ganciclovir to treat it, and once you’re stable, we’ll switch to oral valcyte.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make me feel better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, most patients start feeling improvement within a few days. We’ll monitor your viral load to make sure it’s going down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your labs. Your hemoglobin is low—7.5—so you’re anemic. That’s contributing to your dizziness and fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic before. Will I need a transfusion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to give you a unit of blood now to help with your symptoms. We may need more depending on how your levels respond.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I understand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine test showed a lot of white blood cells and bacteria. We’ve identified Enterococcus faecium, which means you have a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I don’t have burning or frequency. Is that still possible?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with your history. Your immune system is suppressed, so symptoms can be subtle. We started ceftriaxone, but we may need to switch antibiotics based on sensitivities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I’m allergic to vancomycin. Is that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the bacteria is sensitive to vancomycin, but we won’t use it because of your allergy. We’re switching to linezolid, which is safe for you and effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your kidney. There’s mild swelling in the collecting system, but no major blockage. The stent is in place, and your blood flow looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my creatinine is going up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. We also see muddy brown casts in your urine, which suggest acute tubular necrosis—kidney injury from low blood pressure before admission. But it’s not improving as expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my transplant kidney is damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stressed. We’re also checking for BK virus, which can affect transplant kidneys. Your blood level was already elevated—4,858 copies, well above normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that make it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. We’re monitoring it. The nephrostomy tube was capped, but we’re going to uncap it to help with drainage and possibly reduce strain on the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat CMV level is down to 1,440 copies—great improvement. Your symptoms are also better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What about my kidney?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, your creatinine is still rising. It’s now 3.6. We’re concerned your kidney isn’t recovering, and you may need to restart dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was hoping to avoid that. Is it permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. It could be temporary while we treat the infections and stabilize you. But we need access, and your fistula has a known narrowing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember I had that fixed before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll do a fistulogram to open it up, then start dialysis. You’ll go three times a week as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do what’s needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with the fistulogram yesterday. They opened up the blockages in your fistula, and the flow is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt fine afterward. When do I start dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today. You’ll have three sessions before discharge. We’re also continuing valcyte for CMV and linezolid for the UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I need the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ten days total. You’ve had four, so six more after discharge. We’ll send prescriptions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rhythm changed. You went into atrial fibrillation with a fast rate. We restarted your metoprolol, and it’s under control now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel my heart racing yesterday. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. We held your metoprolol earlier due to low blood pressure, but now that you’re stable, we’ve restarted it at your usual dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood thinner?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held warfarin before the fistulogram, so your INR dropped to 1.3. You’ll get 2 mg today, then go back to 1 mg daily. The dialysis center will check your INR and adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed white patches in your mouth. That’s thrush, a fungal infection. We’re starting nystatin swish and swallow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: From being on so many meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Immunosuppression and antibiotics can allow yeast to grow. It should clear up in a couple of weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your CMV is improving, the infection is being treated, and you’ve had three dialysis sessions. We’re ready to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue valcyte every other day, linezolid twice daily for six more days, and dialysis three times a week. Your tacrolimus dose is now 2.5 mg twice daily—we lowered it because levels were high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the omeprazole? I’ve been on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched to ranitidine because omeprazole might affect your kidney. We want to reduce any extra strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make the change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your transplant team will decide if your kidney recovers. If not, they may consider a biopsy. The BK virus results are still pending, so we’ll follow up on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep all my appointments. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your hemoglobin improved slightly after transfusions, but not as much as we hoped. We think some of the blood may have broken down during infusion due to the small IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s strange. But I do feel less dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what matters. We’ll keep monitoring your levels as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we’re sending you home with Nephrocaps, a vitamin for dialysis patients. And zofran for nausea if you need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll take them as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nephrostomy tube is draining well, and your abdomen is soft. No signs of new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any pain there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Keep the site clean and dry. Call if you notice redness, swelling, or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your EKG. You’re in atrial fibrillation, but your rate is controlled. Keep taking your amiodarone and metoprolol as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1 mg daily starting tomorrow. Get your INR checked at dialysis and let them adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your discharge papers are ready. You’ll go home with clear instructions and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I feel ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re doing better. Take it easy, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your albumin is low, and you’ve lost some weight. Try to eat small, frequent meals. The dietitian can help with a plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll work on that. Nausea has been an issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use the zofran as needed. And the ranitidine may help with appetite by reducing reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll follow up with your transplant team. They’ll decide next steps based on your kidney function and BK virus results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep in close contact with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re on the right path. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, I'm Dr. Lee. You were admitted with chest pain and shortness of breath. We think it's due to fluid overload. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still a bit breathless, especially when I lie down. My legs are swollen too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your chest X-ray shows pulmonary edema—fluid in the lungs. We’ve started you on dialysis to remove the extra fluid. That should help your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I got fluid overload after stopping my meds. Is that what happened again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Your kidney function has been unstable since your transplant. We’re also seeing that your heart isn’t pumping as efficiently, which adds to the fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart? I thought it was just my kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart is affected too. You have mild heart failure, and we saw on the EKG that you’re in atrial fibrillation again. That can make your heart less efficient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I was doing so well on my rhythm meds. Shouldn’t we restart the beta-blocker?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re holding off for now because your blood pressure is borderline. Once you’re more stable on dialysis, we’ll adjust your metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my transplant kidney? I keep getting infections from it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about that too. Your CMV is now undetectable, which is good, but your blood counts are low—platelets, white cells, and hemoglobin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low counts? Is that from the transplant meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We think medications like linezolid and ranitidine may be contributing. We’ve stopped both. We’re also lowering your tacrolimus dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so tired. Is that from the anemia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin is low. But since you’re on dialysis, you can get epoetin at your sessions to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had to intubate you last night. You developed sudden respiratory distress. It was likely flash pulmonary edema triggered by your atrial fibrillation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember that. Was I in danger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was serious, but we managed it. You’re off the ventilator now. We used ultrafiltration during dialysis to pull off more fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better breathing now. But my heart is still racing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still in afib and tachycardic—heart rate in the 120s. We’ve increased your metoprolol to 25 mg twice daily to help slow it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my blood pressure during dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. We’ll monitor closely. Your nephrologist and cardiologist may need to coordinate on the right dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows improvement in lung fluid. Your pleural effusions are also decreasing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I can breathe deeper now. What about my heart ultrasound?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The echo shows your heart muscle is thickened, and you have moderate mitral regurgitation. The pressure in your lungs is elevated, which we call pulmonary hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the fluid or the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely a combination. Chronic kidney disease and heart strain both contribute. We’re managing it with fluid removal and heart rate control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back. One showed coagulase-negative staph, but it’s likely a contaminant since only one bottle grew it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No sign of active infection. Your urine culture also showed mixed flora, likely contamination. No antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelet count is improving—up to 150,000. Your white count and hemoglobin are also rising. This suggests the medication changes are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about my immune system.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are too. We’ve restarted dapsone but not ranitidine. We’ll keep your immunosuppressants lower for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV viral load is undetectable. That’s excellent. We’ll continue valganciclovir to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. That was making me so sick last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a kidney biopsy to check the transplant. It’s important to see if there’s rejection or ongoing infection damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do we really need that? I’m tired of being poked. And I’m not sure I want to keep the kidney.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But we need to know what’s going on before making big decisions. The biopsy will help guide whether to keep or remove the graft.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I want to talk to my nephrologist and surgeon after this. I’m done with these infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ve scheduled that discussion for after discharge. For now, we’ll proceed with the biopsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy was successful. Preliminary results show chronic inflammation and scarring, but we can’t tell yet if it’s from infection or rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we still don’t know what’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not fully. The final pathology will take a few more days. But your urine output from the nephrostomy is good, so the kidney is still functioning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is low—only 1.1. We restarted warfarin after the biopsy, but it’s not therapeutic yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shouldn’t I be on heparin until it kicks in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We decided not to bridge because your stroke risk is moderate. But you’ll need frequent INR checks at dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure they fax the results to my doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. No oxygen, walking independently, and your labs are stable. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped ranitidine. Tacrolimus is now 0.5 mg three times a day. Metoprolol is 25 mg twice daily. All your other meds continue as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1 mg daily. Get your INR checked on your next two dialysis days and fax the results to your nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still want to talk about removing the transplant. It’s causing me more harm than good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ve set up appointments with your nephrologist and transplant surgeon. They’ll review the final biopsy and discuss your options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just want to feel better and stop being in and out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge. You look strong, your breathing is good, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for shortness of breath, chest pain, or swelling. Keep your nephrostomy clean and monitor output. And don’t miss your INR checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my doctors. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see how things go after your specialist visits.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you’ve been feeling nauseous and vomited after dinner last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I felt sick to my stomach and threw up once. I haven’t eaten much since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no chest pain or trouble breathing. Just the nausea and some dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I notice you had a cold a week ago—sneezing, congestion, cough. Is that better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s improving. My family had it too—my grandchildren and son-in-law—but no one had a fever or stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We also see your INR came back high at 3.8. That’s related to your warfarin. We’ll hold that for now to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know it was that high. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this moment. We’re monitoring it. We’ll restart warfarin once it’s safer. Your heart rhythm is still irregular, so we’re keeping you on amiodarone and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve been dizzy lately, especially after dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw you couldn’t tolerate ultrafiltration last time. We’ve stopped your furosemide to help stabilize your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so I should stop taking that pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct, we’re discontinuing it for now. We don’t want to drop your blood pressure too low, especially with your heart rhythm issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the nausea? Do you know what’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, it’s viral gastroenteritis—like a stomach bug. You’ve been around sick family, and you’re immunosuppressed, so we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. And my cough? It’s still a bit there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested for flu—both A and B—and it was negative. We’ll treat your cough with guaifenesin to help loosen the mucus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can take that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. Your urine test showed an infection—Enterococcus. It’s sensitive to vancomycin, which we can use since you’re allergic to penicillin and sulfa.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your transplant history. We’ll treat it with vancomycin during your dialysis sessions for about two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get it through my dialysis line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’ll be given slowly during each session. We’ll also check trough levels to make sure the dose is right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You just finished your first dialysis session. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit tired, but the nausea is better. No dizziness this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Your labs are improving—creatinine is down from 2.7 to 2.4, and your electrolytes are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my INR? Is it still high?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s still elevated, so we’re holding warfarin. We’ll check it again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid in the lungs. Just some mild, stable changes from old scarring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So my breathing is okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, lungs are clear. Your heart rhythm is still irregular, but stable. We’re continuing your amiodarone and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant kidney? I know it’s not working anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. The biopsy showed chronic damage. We’re still discussing with your nephrologist whether removal is needed. No decision yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about more infections. It’s been a long road.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re monitoring for CMV, BK, and EBV viruses. So far, CMV is not detected. The other results are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your nausea is gone, and you’re eating well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual meds except furosemide—we’re stopping that. Hold warfarin until your INR is checked. Take guaifenesin for cough as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get five more doses during dialysis. Your kidney doctor will arrange it. Also, check your INR on ___ and call Dr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep following up with your specialists. We’ll send all results to them. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgeons. You’re here today for a planned procedure on your transplanted kidney, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. They told me it’s called a coil embolization. I’m a bit nervous—what exactly does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. It’s a minimally invasive procedure where we block the blood flow to your failed transplant kidney using small metal coils. This helps avoid a major surgery to remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so it’s not being taken out? I thought they might have to cut it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Because of your prior abdominal surgeries and mesh repair, removing it surgically could be risky. This is a safer option to let the kidney shrink over time without infection or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Will I feel anything during the procedure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be given sedation, so you’ll be very relaxed and won’t feel pain. We’ll go through a small puncture in your groin to reach the artery. It usually takes about an hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better than open surgery. What about after? Will I be here long?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to stay flat in bed for a few hours to prevent bleeding at the site. Then, if all goes well, you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I do have a lot of medical history—kidney transplant, heart issues, thyroid—will that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your history. Your atrial fibrillation and thyroid condition are stable. We’ll continue your usual meds, except for a few adjustments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transplant team recommended stopping Myfortic and starting a short course of steroids to help with inflammation. You’ll also keep taking tacrolimus as usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been on Myfortic for years. Is it safe to stop?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because the transplant kidney isn’t working anymore, we don’t need strong immunosuppression. The steroid taper will help your body adjust.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my warfarin? I’ve been off it since my last hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart it soon—your team plans for you to take 4 mg on Thursday, then follow up with your nephrologist for dosing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good, I was worried about my stroke risk with atrial fib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re balancing bleeding and clotting risks carefully. Now, let’s get you prepped for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You did well yesterday with the coil embolization. No complications, and the site looks clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I felt a little pressure but no pain. How long do I need to stay in bed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve already completed the 4-hour bed rest. You can sit up and walk now. We’ll monitor your blood pressure and the groin site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I walked a little earlier—felt fine. But my blood pressure drops after dialysis. I take midodrine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nephrology reviewed that. They’ll contact your nephrologist to adjust your midodrine if needed. For now, keep taking it as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I just get anxious when my BP drops too low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. We’ll keep an eye on it. You also had dialysis yesterday as scheduled?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in the afternoon. I felt a bit weak afterward, but better by evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. Your labs this morning are stable—creatinine is 4.4, which is expected since you’re on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood count? I’ve been anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hemoglobin is 9.6, a bit low but stable. No signs of bleeding. We’ll monitor it at your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re preparing your discharge orders. You’re doing well—eating, walking, no pain or fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, except Myfortic is stopped. You’ll take prednisone for six days—40 mg for three days, then 20 mg for three—then stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, short course. And tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three 0.5 mg capsules every 12 hours. Keep taking your other meds: amiodarone, levothyroxine, pravastatin, and valganciclovir twice a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 4 mg on Thursday. Your INR will be checked soon after. Don’t miss that follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. What about the incision? I don’t even have a big cut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a small puncture. Keep it clean and dry. You can shower, but no baths or swimming until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I have pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Acetaminophen for mild pain. Oxycodone if needed, but don’t drive while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When should I call the doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop fever over 101.5, severe pain, redness at the site, chest pain, or trouble breathing. Also, if you vomit and can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ll follow up with my nephrologist and transplant team?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll monitor your kidney function, INR, and adjust meds as needed. You’re doing well—this was a success.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel relieved this is done without major surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll discharge you in a couple of hours. Keep walking daily, no heavy lifting until your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Your discharge papers are ready. You can go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. See you at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you noticed some blood in your nephrostomy tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It was a small amount, less than half a cup, and it looked like blood. But no pain or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for letting us know. Given your recent embolization, we want to make sure there’s no infection or bleeding issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt fine after the procedure last week. Just this surprise with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve ordered a renal ultrasound to check the transplant kidney and will send a sample from the tube for testing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. You’re not running a fever, and your vitals are stable. But we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound is back. It shows no normal arterial flow, which is expected after embolization. But there are some small gas pockets, which can happen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gas? Like infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your white blood cell count is elevated, so we’re starting one dose of vancomycin tonight as a precaution.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait for the culture from your tube. If it shows infection, we’ll adjust treatment. Blood cultures were drawn and came back clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The lab results are in. The sample from your nephrostomy tube grew VRE—vancomycin-resistant enterococcus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I’ve heard of VRE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a resistant bacteria, but since you’re not showing signs of active infection and your WBC is improving, we don’t need more antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens to the tube?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We plan to remove it tomorrow. Since the embolization has done its job, the tube is no longer needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s usually quick and well-tolerated. We’ll give you some mild sedation if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your hemodialysis is scheduled for noon today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common. We’ll keep you on docusate. Also, we’re holding your metoprolol on dialysis days because of low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my amiodarone and warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on amiodarone for your atrial flutter. Warfarin was paused but will be restarted before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did dialysis go? Any cramping or dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little dizzy, but they stopped early. Only removed one liter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re starting midodrine before dialysis—it helps with blood pressure so more fluid can be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your white count has come down to 10.5—much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the vancomycin helped?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, even though the bacteria was resistant, a single dose may have helped control any early spread.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone? I’m on 20 mg now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on the taper after the embolization. Just two more days, then stop. It helps reduce inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on tacrolimus twice daily. Since the kidney is embolized, we’re keeping immunosuppression minimal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to remove the nephrostomy tube now. Any questions before we proceed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will there be a dressing after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll cover it for a few days. Keep it dry. You can shower, but no baths or swimming yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tube is out. Site looks clean and dry. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Later today. We’ll finalize your discharge meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Continue all your usual dialysis routines, fluid limits, and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, restart warfarin as prescribed—three 1 mg tablets daily. Your INR will be checked at dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. Avoid heavy lifting for now. Call the transplant office if you see redness, swelling, or drainage at the site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And finish the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take 20 mg today and tomorrow, then stop. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Safe travels home, and see your nephrologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good evening. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in because you had a high fever and chills. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up shaking and felt very hot. My temperature was 102. I’ve been on dialysis and have a history of kidney issues, so I thought I should come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. We’ve run some tests. Your blood work shows signs of infection—your white blood cell count is low, and we’ve started you on antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious? I’ve had infections before, but this one felt different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we caught it early. You’re septic, meaning the infection is in your bloodstream. But you’re stable now, and we’re treating it aggressively.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t realize it was that bad. What’s causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still figuring that out. One possibility is your gallbladder—your CT scan showed some gallstones and a slightly dilated bile duct.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had gallstones before, but never caused a fever like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: True, but in patients like you—on dialysis and immunosuppressed—small issues can become bigger. We also checked your kidney transplant site. It looks swollen but no abscess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that coil embolization recently. Could that be related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that, but no signs of infection there. Your urine culture came back negative, so it’s not a urinary source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So where’s the infection coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. But your blood cultures are growing E. coli. That’s a clue. We’re thinking it might be from a cyst—liver or pancreatic—since you have polycystic kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A cyst? Like a fluid-filled sac?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’re common in your condition. Sometimes they get infected, and it’s hard to see on scans. We’ve called infectious disease to help us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re transferring you to our main campus so you’re closer to dialysis. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still tired, but the chills stopped. Are we any closer to finding the source?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. But we’re doing an endoscopic ultrasound tomorrow to look at your bile duct and pancreas more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you’ll sleep through it. It’s the best way to check for stones or cysts that might be causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started your dialysis today and given your first dose of linezolid and cefepime. We’ll keep you on these until we know more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember those antibiotics. I’ve been on so many.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a lot. But we’re being cautious. Your heart rhythm also changed earlier—brief atrial fibrillation with fast rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I thought amiodarone was controlling it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your amiodarone and metoprolol because your blood pressure was low. But we restarted metoprolol at half dose, and you’ve returned to normal rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want another cardioversion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You spiked a fever again last night, but it came down with meds. Blood cultures are still pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt hot again. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not uncommon early on. But we’re watching closely. Your INR was low, so we held warfarin temporarily in case you need a procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot about that. I don’t want a clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart it soon. For now, safety first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your EUS is done. No stones blocking the bile duct. But we did see a 1.9 cm cyst in your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the source?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. It’s small and not connected to the duct, so we won’t drain it. But infectious disease thinks it could be infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we treat it just in case?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They recommend switching to IV ceftazidime for three weeks, given during dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics I’m on now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll stop linezolid and cefepime. Ceftazidime is better targeted for E. coli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a tagged white blood cell scan to look for hidden infection. It didn’t show a clear source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still a guess?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: More of an educated one. In patients with polycystic disease, cyst infections can be silent and hard to detect. The treatment is the same—antibiotics that penetrate cysts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been fever-free since yesterday. That’s a great sign the new antibiotic is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Still weak, but not shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped, so we gave one unit of blood during dialysis yesterday. It’s expected with chronic kidney disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had transfusions before. I hope I don’t need more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor it. Your potassium was high on admission, but it’s improved with dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV test came back negative. That’s good—we can rule that out as a cause of fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had CMV before. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking everything. Your liver enzymes are normal, so no sign of hepatitis or cholangitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had two days without fever, and your latest blood cultures are negative. That means the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly in two days. You’ll continue ceftazidime with each dialysis session for three weeks total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most stay the same. Warfarin is back, and your INR is therapeutic at 2.6. Metoprolol is at half dose, held on dialysis days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re doing well—afebrile, eating, and strong enough to walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see infectious disease in the clinic after your last antibiotic dose. And repeat the pancreatic cyst imaging in six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another EUS?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Either EUS or an MRCP. Your team will decide. For now, focus on finishing antibiotics and staying well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send the antibiotic to your dialysis center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried this fever wouldn’t go away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident you’re on the right track. Keep taking your meds, and call if you develop fever, pain, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the weekly labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—CBC, basic metabolic panel, and liver tests every week at dialysis. Fax them to your clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure they do. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the emergency room because you suddenly had trouble breathing. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was napping after lunch and woke up gasping. I couldn’t catch my breath. I didn’t have chest pain or fever, just very short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your oxygen and it was very low—only 50% on room air. Your chest X-ray shows fluid in your lungs, which is likely from heart failure and fluid overload.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. But I’ve been taking my medicines and doing dialysis. Could the salty meal have caused this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, extra salt can make your body hold onto fluid, especially with kidney disease. We’ve started you on oxygen and a nitroglycerin drip to ease the pressure on your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be okay? I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re in good hands. We’ve called your dialysis team for urgent treatment to remove the extra fluid. That should help your breathing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve had dialysis for years, but never felt like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is a flare-up of heart failure, likely worsened by fluid buildup. We’re admitting you to the ICU for close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your first dialysis session went well. Your oxygen improved, and your breathing is much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel better. But I was on oxygen again overnight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your oxygen dipped to 88% while you were sleeping. It came back up with a little extra oxygen. We’re watching for possible sleep apnea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sleep apnea? I snore sometimes, but never thought much of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common in patients like you. We’ll recommend a sleep study after discharge to check for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows big improvement. The fluid in your lungs is clearing up thanks to dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But the X-ray mentioned an opacity in my lung. Is that infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started antibiotics just in case, but you’ve had no fever or cough. The radiologist thinks it’s more likely uneven fluid buildup than pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So will you stop the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since you’re not showing signs of infection and your blood cultures have no growth so far, we’ll discontinue them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want to take more meds than I need.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an echocardiogram yesterday. It shows your heart’s pumping function is okay, but your mitral valve leak has gotten worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Worse? I’ve had mitral regurgitation for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but now it’s moderate to severe. That can contribute to fluid backing up into your lungs. You’ll need to see your cardiologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When should I go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend within a week. They’ll decide if you need further testing or treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call them today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your kidney function is stable on dialysis. We’re continuing your usual meds like tacrolimus and sevelamer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take lisinopril, but I stopped because of the cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. We considered another blood pressure med, but with your dialysis, it might drop too low. So we’re holding off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I trust your judgment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another dialysis session yesterday. We’re trying to get you to your ‘dry weight’—your ideal fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter already. Less swelling in my legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. During that session, your heart briefly went into atrial fibrillation, but it corrected on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not this time. You stayed stable, and your rate was controlled. We’ll keep you on amiodarone and metoprolol as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your INR is in range. You’ll continue warfarin for stroke prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we reviewed your prior endoscopic ultrasound. You have a pancreatic cyst, about 1.9 cm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are benign, but we recommend a repeat EUS or MRCP in six months to monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll schedule that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re ready to go home today. Your breathing is stable, and your fluid status is much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are the same. We’re lowering your warfarin dose—hold it today, take 2 mg tomorrow, then follow your dialysis center’s instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my levothyroxine is now 75 mcg?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it’s 75 mcg total, but you’ll take 1.5 of the 50 mcg tablets daily. We reduced it slightly due to your thyroid levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll adjust that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, use the lidocaine patch for any arm pain from your fistula. And please follow up with your cardiologist, sleep doctor, and dialysis team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, or swelling comes back. Otherwise, take care and rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send all your records to your doctors. Someone from the dialysis center will call to check in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy, avoid salty foods, and weigh yourself daily. Any sudden gain, let your team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I learned my lesson with that salty meal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Small changes make a big difference. You’ve done well this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lucky to have such a good team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re glad you’re on the mend. Discharge papers are ready. A nurse will go over everything before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. I’m ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You came in with fevers—can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I started feeling feverish last night while I was on vacation. I thought it was from being in the sun too long, but the fever kept coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How high did it get? Any chills or sweats?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Over 100, and yes, I had rigors—shaking and sweating. I took Tylenol, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any sore throat, cough, or pain anywhere?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sore throat and headache. And I noticed my transplant area in the lower right belly feels tender now—never felt like that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. We also saw on your EKG you were in atrial fibrillation with a fast heart rate. Did you feel your heart racing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a little flutter, but not too bad. I’ve had afib before, so I wasn’t too worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you fluids and a small dose of metoprolol, and your heart rate came down. That’s good. We’re going to run some tests to find the source of the fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had E. coli in my blood before—could it be back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. We’re checking blood and urine cultures. We also did a CT scan of your abdomen. It showed some increased inflammation around your old transplant kidney. We can’t rule out infection, but it could also be from ongoing rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So do I need surgery for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. The transplant team reviewed it and said removal isn’t needed yet. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my calcium? I’ve been tingling in my fingers and around my mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your calcium is low—6.0, and your ionized calcium is also low. That explains the tingling. It’s likely from your cinacalcet. We’re holding that medicine and giving you calcium supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help quickly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you an IV dose and started oral calcium. Your levels are already improving. We’ll check again tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture grew E. coli, but it’s resistant to ciprofloxacin. The rest of your cultures—blood, throat, CMV—are negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is it a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
